name: Lithops
description: Native to the rocky deserts of southern Africa, Lithops are among the most unusual plants in existence - they've evolved to look exactly like small pebbles or stones as camouflage from grazing animals. Each plant consists of just two thick, fused leaves separated by a fissure from which flowers and new leaves emerge. The flat or slightly rounded tops often have intricate patterns and colors mimicking the stones in their habitat. Growing only 1-2 inches tall, they're miniature marvels of evolution. However, Lithops are notoriously difficult because they follow a specific annual cycle and require NO water during certain periods. Watering at the wrong time is fatal. They're strictly for experienced succulent growers who can resist the urge to water and understand their unique lifecycle.
toxicity: Non-toxic to cats, dogs and horses.
careInstructions: CRITICAL: Follow the annual water cycle exactly - wrong timing kills the plant
Late spring to early summer: water when the soil is completely dry
Mid-summer (dormant): stop watering - if it shrivels badly, just moisten the top half-inch of soil
Late summer to fall (growing and flowering): water about every 2 weeks, letting the soil dry completely in between
Winter to early spring: no water at all, until the old leaves have dried to papery husks
Give it 4-5 hours of direct morning sun with some afternoon shade - a south or unobstructed east window
Use extremely well-draining mineral mix (50%+ pumice/grit)
Never water during splitting period or old leaves won't dry properly
commonProblems: Overwatering: Most common cause of death - leads to rot and bursting
Watering during splitting: Prevents old leaves from drying, causes rot
Soft, mushy plants: Fatal overwatering - usually cannot be saved
Stretching (etiolation): Insufficient light - needs maximum sun
Not splitting: May be too young or not getting proper rest period
Bursting: Overwatering causing cells to rupture - usually fatal

fertilizing.tip: Fertilize sparingly with a low-nitrogen, high-potassium fertilizer

repotting.tip: Use a pot 3-5 inches deep — the roots are extensive. It can stay in the same pot for 10-20 years.
repotting.soil: Cactus mix, or potting mix with sharp sand, perlite or grit

whatsNormal: Each year a new pair of leaves grows from the central slit while the old pair shrivels to a papery husk.
Flowers in fall and early winter from the slit between the leaves; the flowers open on sunny afternoons.
Shrinking and shriveling during summer dormancy is normal.
Stretching, leaning or turning greenish means it needs more light — increase it gradually to avoid sunburn.

propagation.tip: Divide multi-headed plants, or grow from seed in summer.

flags.note: Toxicity: Wisconsin Extension says Lithops are non-toxic to humans and pets; ASPCA lists Lithops naureeniae as non-toxic to cats, dogs and horses.

Watering cycle: sprouthub's schedule model can't express "no water at all" for winter to early spring. Set the dormant-season interval to 90 days as the closest fit; Lithops may need special handling in the app.
Fertilizer interval (13-26 weeks) is our estimate — Wisconsin only says "sparingly".

Changed: the old guide said to water every 3-4 weeks in winter; both sources say no water from winter to early spring. Added the late-spring watering window, every-2-weeks fall watering, and morning-sun-plus-afternoon-shade light.
